claim: Phrenic motor neurons (MNs) provide the sole innervation to the diaphragm, a muscle that is critical for bringing oxygenated air into the lungs during inspiration.
source: PMC neurons provide the sole innervation to the diaphragm, a muscle that is critical for bringing oxygenated air into the lungs during inspiration (Greer, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Greer, 2012, which provides external scholarly support for this statement.

claim: The molecular mechanisms that underlie rVRG–PMC connectivity are largely unknown.
source: While the ability of phrenic motor neurons (MNs) to receive and integrate descending inputs from the rVRG is essential for breathing, the molecular mechanisms that underlie rVRG–PMC connectivity are largely unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field, representing a knowledge gap.

claim: Phrenic MNs express a unique combination of cell surface adhesion molecules that could potentially serve as molecular recognition tags for descending brainstem axons.
source: Phrenic MNs express a unique combination of cell surface adhesion molecules that could potentially serve as molecular recognition tags for descending brainstem axons (Machado et al., 2014; Vagnozzi et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Machado et al., 2014; Vagnozzi et al., 2020) and involves speculation about potential function.

claim: Phrenic MNs express the type I N-cadherin (Cdh2) and the type II cadherins Cdh6, 9, 10, 11, and 22 at e13.5.
source: We previously conducted in situ hybridization for all type I and II cadherins in the PMC at e13.5, a timepoint at which early phrenic MN topography is already established, but synapse formation has yet to occur. We found that phrenic MNs express the type I N-cadherin (Cdh2) and the type II cadherins Cdh6, 9, 10, 11, and 22 (Vagnozzi et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Vagnozzi et al., 2020) describing in situ hybridization experiments.

claim: Cdh9 and 10 are remarkably specific to phrenic MNs.
source: While the type I cadherin N-cadherin and the type II cadherins Cdh6, 11, and 22 show broad expression in either all neurons (N-cadherin) or all MNs (6, 11, and 22), Cdh9 and 10 are remarkably specific to phrenic MNs (Figure 1a, Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1a and Figure 1—figure supplement 1a, which show expression patterns.

claim: Loss of cadherin signaling specifically in MNs, via inactivation of β- and γ-catenin, leads to embryonic lethality.
source: We also found that loss of cadherin signaling specifically in MNs, via inactivation of the cadherin obligate intracellular partners β- and γ-catenin, leads to embryonic lethality, suggesting a critical role for cadherins in phrenic MN function (Vagnozzi et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Vagnozzi et al., 2020) describing genetic experiments.

claim: PMC-expressed cadherins 6, 9 and 10 form a specificity group, preferentially interacting with each other compared to other cadherins.
source: PMC-expressed cadherins 6, 9 and 10 form a specificity group, preferentially interacting with each other compared to other cadherins (Brasch et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Brasch et al., 2018, which provides external evidence for cadherin interactions.

claim: Neonatal (P2) 6910KO mice have normal minute ventilation and live to adulthood.
source: Surprisingly, we found that neonatal (P2) 6910KO mice have normal minute ventilation (volume of air inhaled per minute) and live to adulthood (Figure 1—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 2b showing plethysmography data.

claim: Both NMN∆ and NMNΔ6910KO mice die within 24 hr of birth.
source: We found that both NMN∆ and NMNΔ6910KO mice die within 24 hr of birth.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: NMNΔ6910KO mice appear cyanotic and gasp for breath.
source: While NMN∆ mice likely die due to deficiencies in feeding (data not shown), NMNΔ6910KO mice appear cyanotic and gasp for breath (Figure 1b, Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1b and Figure 1—video 1 showing phenotypic observations.

claim: NMNΔ6910KO mice display a 40% reduction in minute ventilation.
source: Together, these two parameters combined resulted in a 40% reduction in minute ventilation (volume of air inhaled per minute, Figure 1e), indicating that NMNΔ6910KO mice have severe respiratory insufficiency and die due to respiratory failure.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1e showing plethysmography quantification.

claim: NMNΔ6910KO mice have severe respiratory insufficiency and die due to respiratory failure.
source: Together, these two parameters combined resulted in a 40% reduction in minute ventilation (volume of air inhaled per minute, Figure 1e), indicating that NMNΔ6910KO mice have severe respiratory insufficiency and die due to respiratory failure.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the measured reduction in minute ventilation and the observed phenotype.

claim: The combinatorial activity of N-cadherin, Cdh6, 9, and 10 is required for proper respiratory behavior.
source: Our findings indicate that the combinatorial activity of N-cadherin, Cdh6, 9, and 10 is required for proper respiratory behavior.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations on NMNΔ6910KO mice.

claim: 6910KO mice have normal diaphragm innervation.
source: We found that 6910KO mice have normal diaphragm innervation, while NMNΔ mice have a slight decrease (~16%) in terminal arborization in the ventral diaphragm (Figure 1—figure supplement 3a–c).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 3a–c showing diaphragm innervation analysis.

claim: NMNΔ mice have a slight decrease (~16%) in terminal arborization in the ventral diaphragm.
source: We found that 6910KO mice have normal diaphragm innervation, while NMNΔ mice have a slight decrease (~16%) in terminal arborization in the ventral diaphragm (Figure 1—figure supplement 3a–c).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 3a–c showing quantified diaphragm innervation.

claim: NMNΔ6910KO mice show a significant reduction in diaphragm innervation (~30% loss of innervation), which is more pronounced at the ventral part of the diaphragm.
source: NMNΔ6910KO mice show a significant reduction in diaphragm innervation (~30% loss of innervation), which is more pronounced at the ventral part of the diaphragm (Figure 1—figure supplement 3a–c, arrows).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 3a–c showing quantified diaphragm innervation.

claim: The phrenic nerve retains its ability to contract the diaphragm in NMNΔ6910KO mice.
source: We stimulated the phrenic nerve in reduced medullary-brainstem preparations at e18.5/P0, and observed similar contractions in control and NMNΔ6910KO mice, indicating functional NMJs and suggesting that the phrenic nerve retains its ability to contract the diaphragm in NMNΔ6910KO mice (Figure 1—video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1—video 2 showing nerve stimulation experiments.

claim: As little as 40% diaphragm innervation is sufficient for survival.
source: While diaphragm innervation defects may partially contribute to the tidal volume reduction and perinatal lethality in NMNΔ6910KO mice, we have previously shown that as little as 40% diaphragm innervation is sufficient for survival (Vagnozzi et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Vagnozzi et al., 2020).

claim: It is unlikely that ~30% reduction in diaphragm innervation solely underlies the respiratory insufficiency seen upon cadherin inactivation.
source: Therefore, it is unlikely that ~30% reduction in diaphragm innervation solely underlies the respiratory insufficiency seen upon cadherin inactivation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison between the observed reduction and previously established sufficiency thresholds.

claim: Early phrenic MN specification is unperturbed in control, 6910KO, NMNΔ, and NMNΔ6910KO mice.
source: We found a cluster of Scip + MNs in the ventral cervical spinal cord of control, 6910KO, NMNΔ, and NMNΔ6910KO mice, indicating that early phrenic MN specification is unperturbed (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1a showing Scip+ MN labeling.

claim: NMNΔ and NMNΔ6910KO mice occasionally show migratory defects, where a few phrenic MNs remain close to the midline instead of fully migrating.
source: We noted that both NMNΔ and NMNΔ6910KO mice occasionally show migratory defects, where a few phrenic MNs remain close to the midline instead of fully migrating (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b, arrow).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1b showing cell body positions.

claim: NMNΔ and NMNΔ6910KO mice showed a similar decrease in phrenic MN numbers.
source: In addition, NMNΔ and NMNΔ6910KO mice showed a similar decrease in phrenic MN numbers, likely from the loss of trophic support due to the decrease in diaphragm innervation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1c showing quantification of MN numbers.

claim: Even after substantial MN loss, 50% of surviving phrenic MNs are sufficient to support life.
source: While phrenic MN loss may contribute to the perinatal lethality observed in NMNΔ6910KO mice, we have previously found that, even after substantial MN loss, 50% of surviving phrenic MNs are sufficient to support life (Vagnozzi et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Vagnozzi et al., 2020).

claim: 6910KO mice show no difference in PMC position compared to control.
source: We first examined control and 6910KO mice and found no difference in PMC position (Figure 2a, b, Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2a, b, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1a showing positional analysis.

claim: Both NMNΔ and NMNΔ6910KO mice displayed a significant shift in phrenic MN cell body position, with cell bodies shifting ventrally toward the edge of the spinal cord.
source: Both NMNΔ and NMNΔ6910KO mice displayed a significant shift in phrenic MN cell body position, with cell bodies shifting ventrally toward the edge of the spinal cord (Figure 2c–f, Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2c–f and Figure 2—figure supplement 1a showing positional analysis.

claim: Cell bodies in NMNΔ and NMNΔ6910KO mice overlapped when compared on contour density plots.
source: Cell bodies in NMNΔ and NMNΔ6910KO mice overlapped when compared on contour density plots (Figure 2g, h).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2g, h showing contour density plots.

claim: Control and 6910KO mice are highly similar (r = 0.95) in phrenic MN position.
source: Correlation analysis determined that control and 6910KO mice are highly similar (r = 0.95), as are NMNΔ and NMNΔ6910KO mice (r = 0.96), but each group is dissimilar from the other (r = 0.45–0.54, Figure 2m).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2m showing correlation analysis.

claim: NMNΔ and NMNΔ6910KO mice are highly similar (r = 0.96) in phrenic MN position.
source: Correlation analysis determined that control and 6910KO mice are highly similar (r = 0.95), as are NMNΔ and NMNΔ6910KO mice (r = 0.96), but each group is dissimilar from the other (r = 0.45–0.54, Figure 2m).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2m showing correlation analysis.

claim: N-cadherin has a predominant function in phrenic MN topography.
source: Therefore, 6910KO mice show no positional changes, while NMNΔ and NMNΔ6910KO mice display similar changes in cell body position, suggesting a predominant function for N-cadherin in phrenic MN topography.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of positional changes across different genotypes.

claim: In control and 6910KO mice, phrenic MN dendrites branch out in dorsolateral to ventromedial directions.
source: In control and 6910KO mice, phrenic MN dendrites branch out in dorsolateral to ventromedial directions (Figure 3a, c, Figure 3—figure supplement 1a, b).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 3a, c, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1a, b showing DiI-labeled dendrites.

claim: In NMNΔ mice, dendrites appear ventralized and do not reach as far in the dorsolateral direction.
source: In NMNΔ mice, dendrites appear ventralized and do not reach as far in the dorsolateral direction (Figure 3e, Figure 3—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 3e and Figure 3—figure supplement 1c showing DiI-labeled dendrites.

claim: Phrenic MN dendrites in NMNΔ6910KO mice show a dramatic reorganization, exhibiting both ventralization and defasciculation.
source: Phrenic MN dendrites in NMNΔ6910KO mice show a dramatic reorganization, exhibiting both ventralization and defasciculation (Figure 3g, Figure 3—figure supplement 1d, e).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 3g and Figure 3—figure supplement 1d, e showing DiI-labeled dendrites.

claim: In control and 6910KO mice, the main contributions to dendritic fluorescence intensity came from dorsolaterally projecting dendrites (0–90 degrees), representing 40–45% of the overall dendritic intensity.
source: In control and 6910KO mice, the main contributions to dendritic fluorescence intensity came from dorsolaterally projecting dendrites (0–90 degrees), representing 40–45% of the overall dendritic intensity (Figure 3b, d, i, m).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 3b, d, i, m showing quantified dendritic orientation.

claim: In NMNΔ mice, the intensity of dorsolateral dendrites was maintained.
source: In NMNΔ mice, the intensity of dorsolateral dendrites was maintained (Figure 3f, j, m), while there was an increase in ventral dendrites (Figure 3m).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 3f, j, m showing quantified dendritic orientation.

claim: NMNΔ6910KO mice had a striking reduction in dorsolateral dendrites, with a concomitant increase in ventral dendrites.
source: NMNΔ6910KO mice had a striking reduction in dorsolateral dendrites, with a concomitant increase in ventral dendrites (Figure 3h, k, m).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 3h, k, m showing quantified dendritic orientation.

claim: N-cadherin predominantly acts to restrict the number of ventrally projecting dendrites.
source: When directly comparing NMNΔ and NMNΔ6910KO mice, NMNΔ6910KO mice had a more severe loss of dorsolateral dendrites while both NMNΔ and NMNΔ6910KO mice showed an increase in ventral dendrites, indicating that N-cadherin predominantly acts to restrict the number of ventrally projecting dendrites (Figure 3l, m).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of dendritic orientation across genotypes.

claim: Cadherins N, 6, 9, and 10 collectively control phrenic MN dendritic orientation and topography.
source: Together, these data suggest that cadherins N, 6, 9, and 10 collectively control phrenic MN dendritic orientation and topography, which may contribute to their targeting by presynaptic partners.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the dendritic analysis experiments, with speculation about functional consequences.

claim: Burst duration was similar in control, NMNΔ, 6910KO, and NMNΔ6910KO mice at e18.5/P0.
source: Burst duration, however, was more consistent, and was similar in control, NMNΔ, 6910KO, and NMNΔ6910KO mice (Figure 4b).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 4b showing burst duration measurements.

claim: 70% of NMNΔ6910KO mice display respiratory bursts, while 30% show no bursts throughout the recording period.
source: While 70% of NMNΔ6910KO mice display respiratory bursts, 30% show no bursts throughout the recording period. Respiratory bursts are indicated with magenta arrows.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 4c showing phrenic nerve recordings.

claim: NMNΔ6910KO mice exhibit nearly 70% reduction in normalized integrated burst activity and normalized integrated burst activity over time.
source: After rectifying and integrating the traces, we found a nearly 70% decrease in both total burst activity and burst activity normalized over time in NMNΔ6910KO mice (Figure 4e, f).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 4e, f showing quantified burst activity.

claim: NMNΔ mice show normal burst activity.
source: Notably, NMNΔ mice show normal burst activity, supporting our initial observations that their perinatal death was not due to respiratory failure.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the electrophysiology experiments.

claim: Neither cell body position nor phrenic MN numbers significantly contribute to phrenic MN output.
source: Furthermore, the fact that phrenic MNs maintain their normal activity pattern in NMNΔ mice suggests that neither cell body position nor phrenic MN numbers significantly contribute to phrenic MN output.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that NMNΔ mice have altered cell body position and reduced MN numbers but normal burst activity.

claim: Coordinated activity of both type I and type II cadherins is imperative for robust activation of phrenic MNs during inspiration.
source: Our data also indicate that individual type I and II cadherins are dispensable for normal phrenic MN activity, but that coordinated activity of both types is imperative for robust activation of phrenic MNs during inspiration.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the phenotypes of different cadherin mutants.

claim: Spinal network activity after the addition of picrotoxin and strychnine was similar in control and NMNΔ6910KO mice, both in duration and normalized integrated activity over time.
source: Spinal network activity after the addition of picrotoxin and strychnine was similar in control and NMNΔ6910KO mice, both in duration and normalized integrated activity over time, indicating that phrenic MNs are being activated normally by these propriospinal inputs after cadherin loss (Figure 4h).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 4h showing quantified spinal network activity.

claim: Phrenic MNs are normally integrated into propriospinal circuits in NMNΔ6910KO mice.
source: Our data indicate that phrenic MNs are normally integrated into propriospinal circuits and, despite the reduction in respiratory activity, can be robustly activated by other inputs in NMNΔ6910KO mice.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that spinal network activity is normal in NMNΔ6910KO mice after disinhibition.

claim: There is a selective requirement for cadherin function for phrenic MN activation by descending excitatory inputs.
source: Our results suggest a selective requirement for cadherin function for phrenic MN activation by descending excitatory inputs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the differential effects on respiratory versus propriospinal activity.

claim: rVRG neurons express a complementary cadherin code to phrenic MNs, showing specific and robust expression of Cdh6, Cdh9, and Cdh10.
source: We found that rVRG neurons express a complementary cadherin code to phrenic MNs, showing specific and robust expression of Cdh6, Cdh9, and Cdh10, while N-cadherin is broadly expressed in the brainstem, mirroring the expression pattern seen in the spinal cord (Figure 5a–g).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 5a–g showing in situ hybridization in the brainstem.

claim: 80% of rVRG neurons are cdh9+ (n = 136/195 and 301/335 mCherry + neurons from two mice).
source: We found that 80% of rVRG neurons (n = 136/195 and 301/335 mCherry + neurons from two mice) are also labeled green by Ai3, indicating that the Cdh6/9/10 + neurons we detected in the brainstem at e15.5 likely correspond to the rVRG (Figure 5k, l).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 5k, l showing rabies tracing results with specific cell counts.

claim: Cadherin 6/9/10 expression defines the core motor respiratory circuit.
source: Our results show that cadherin 6/9/10 expression defines the core motor respiratory circuit, raising the possibility that cadherins are required in multiple respiratory neuronal populations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the expression analysis and circuit tracing experiments.

claim: Bγ-catDbx1∆ mice are born alive but die within 24 hr after birth.
source: We found that βγ-catDbx1∆ mice are born alive but die within 24 hr after birth.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiments on βγ-catDbx1∆ mice.

claim: Bγ-catDbx1∆ mice do not show significant changes in respiratory burst frequency or duration.
source: Bγ-catDbx1∆ mice do not show significant changes in respiratory burst frequency or duration (Figure 6b).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 6b showing burst frequency and duration measurements.

claim: βγ-catDbx1∆ mice show a 50% reduction in total burst activity.
source: After rectifying and integrating the traces, we saw a 50% reduction in total burst activity in βγ-catDbx1∆ mice as compared to control (Figure 6d).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 6d showing quantified burst activity.

claim: When comparing βγ-catDbx1∆ mice to NMNΔ6910KO mice, no significant difference in burst activity was seen.
source: When comparing βγ-catDbx1∆ mice to NMNΔ6910KO mice, no significant difference was seen (Figure 6e), suggesting that cadherin function is required both in MNs and Dbx1-derived interneurons for robust respiratory output.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 6e showing comparative burst activity measurements.

claim: Cadherin function is required both in MNs and Dbx1-derived interneurons for robust respiratory output.
source: When comparing βγ-catDbx1∆ mice to NMNΔ6910KO mice, no significant difference was seen (Figure 6e), suggesting that cadherin function is required both in MNs and Dbx1-derived interneurons for robust respiratory output.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of burst activity in different mutants.

claim: A combinatorial cadherin code defines the core respiratory motor circuit.
source: In this study, we find that a combinatorial cadherin code defines the core respiratory motor circuit and that coordinated cadherin function is required in multiple respiratory neuronal populations to drive robust respiratory output and survival (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from all the experimental findings in the manuscript.

claim: Coordinated cadherin function is required in multiple respiratory neuronal populations to drive robust respiratory output and survival.
source: In this study, we find that a combinatorial cadherin code defines the core respiratory motor circuit and that coordinated cadherin function is required in multiple respiratory neuronal populations to drive robust respiratory output and survival (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from all the experimental findings in the manuscript.

claim: MN-specific cadherin deletion alters phrenic MN topography, activity, and breathing behaviors, resulting in death shortly after birth.
source: MN-specific cadherin deletion alters phrenic MN topography, activity, and breathing behaviors, resulting in death shortly after birth.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the findings from NMNΔ6910KO mice experiments.

claim: Dbx1-mediated cadherin inactivation results in diminished phrenic MN output and perinatal death.
source: Similarly, Dbx1-mediated cadherin inactivation also results in diminished phrenic MN output and perinatal death.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the findings from βγ-catDbx1∆ mice experiments.

claim: The respiratory rhythm is initiated by an oscillatory population in the brainstem, the preBötzinger (preBötC) complex.
source: Respiratory rhythmogenesis is initiated by an oscillatory population in the brainstem, the preBötzinger (preBötC) complex (Del Negro et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Del Negro et al., 2018.

claim: This respiratory rhythm is relayed through an area in the brainstem called the rostral Ventral Respiratory Group (rVRG) to Phrenic Motor Column (PMC) neurons in the spinal cord.
source: This respiratory rhythm is relayed through an area in the brainstem called the rostral Ventral Respiratory Group (rVRG) to Phrenic Motor Column (PMC) neurons in the spinal cord (Wu et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wu et al., 2017.

claim: PMC neurons are a specialized subset of MNs confined to the cervical region of the spinal cord.
source: PMC neurons are a specialized subset of MNs confined to the cervical region of the spinal cord.
evidence: This is a statement of established anatomical knowledge.

claim: Phrenic MNs largely eschew propriospinal inputs and instead integrate medullary inputs to produce robust respiratory activity.
source: Unlike the majority of other MN subtypes, they largely eschew propriospinal inputs and instead integrate medullary inputs to produce robust respiratory activity (Wu et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wu et al., 2017.

claim: The transcriptional programs that define molecular features of phrenic MNs which distinguish them from other MN populations during development are beginning to emerge.
source: The transcriptional programs that define molecular features of phrenic MNs which distinguish them from other MN populations during development are beginning to emerge (Chaimowicz et al., 2019; Machado et al., 2014; Philippidou et al., 2012; Vagnozzi et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations describing transcriptional programs.

claim: In the monosynaptic stretch reflex circuit, both MN cell body position and dendritic orientation have been implicated in controlling connectivity patterns during development.
source: In the monosynaptic stretch reflex circuit, where group Ia sensory afferents synapse directly onto the alpha MNs innervating the same muscle with exquisite specificity, both MN cell body position and dendritic orientation have been implicated in controlling connectivity patterns during development (Balaskas et al., 2019; Sürmeli et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Balaskas et al., 2019 and Sürmeli et al., 2011.

claim: The chemoaffinity hypothesis proposes that cell surface homophilic interactions enable matching between synaptic partners.
source: While the long-standing chemoaffinity hypothesis, proposing that cell surface homophilic interactions enable matching between synaptic partners (Sperry, 1963), has been illustrated in the visual and olfactory circuits (Graham and Duan, 2021; Xie et al., 2022), the relative contribution of transmembrane recognition molecules in motor circuits, and to phrenic MN connectivity specifically, is unclear.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Sperry, 1963, Graham and Duan, 2021, and Xie et al., 2022.

claim: Cadherins establish the segregation and settling position of MN cell bodies in the spinal cord.
source: Cadherins establish the segregation and settling position of MN cell bodies in the spinal cord (Demireva et al., 2011; Dewitz et al., 2019; Dewitz et al., 2018; Price et al., 2002), but their contribution to the wiring of motor circuits and their function has not yet been determined.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations describing cadherin function in MN positioning.

claim: In the retina, type II cadherins direct neuronal projections to distinct laminae, thereby dictating synaptic specificity.
source: In the retina, type II cadherins direct neuronal projections to distinct laminae, thereby dictating synaptic specificity (Duan et al., 2014; Duan et al., 2018; Osterhout et al., 2011), while in the hippocampus they establish synaptic fidelity without overtly affecting neuronal morphology (Basu et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on retinal cadherins.

claim: In the hippocampus, type II cadherins establish synaptic fidelity without overtly affecting neuronal morphology.
source: In the retina, type II cadherins direct neuronal projections to distinct laminae, thereby dictating synaptic specificity (Duan et al., 2014; Duan et al., 2018; Osterhout et al., 2011), while in the hippocampus they establish synaptic fidelity without overtly affecting neuronal morphology (Basu et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Basu et al., 2017.

claim: In both the retina and the hippocampus type II cadherins function independently, without any contributions from type I family members.
source: Despite utilizing distinct strategies to establish connectivity, in both the retina and the hippocampus type II cadherins function independently, without any contributions from type I family members.
evidence: This is a statement summarizing findings from previous studies on cadherin function.

claim: Both type I and II cadherins are required for establishing the stereotyped motor pool organization in the spinal cord.
source: In contrast, both type I and II cadherins are required for establishing the stereotyped motor pool organization in the spinal cord.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about cadherin function in the spinal cord.

claim: Type I cadherin N-cadherin can mask the contributions of type II cadherins in controlling MN cell body positioning.
source: It has recently been demonstrated that type I cadherins, such as N-cadherin, can mask the contributions of type II cadherins in controlling MN cell body positioning, raising the possibility that type I and II cadherins may have coordinated functions in other aspects of MN development (Dewitz et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Dewitz et al., 2019.

claim: NMNΔ6910KO mice lack N-cadherin and Cdh6, 9, and 10 expression in all MNs by e11.5.
source: NMNΔ6910KO mice lack N-cadherin and Cdh6, 9, and 10 expression in all MNs by e11.5 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1b showing in situ hybridization.

claim: NMNΔ6910KO mice displayed two different kinds of abnormal respiratory behavior: either fast and shallow breathing, or slow, irregular, gasping behavior.
source: We found that NMNΔ6910KO mice displayed two different kinds of abnormal respiratory behavior: either fast and shallow breathing, or slow, irregular, gasping behavior (Figure 1d).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1d showing plethysmography traces.

claim: During the periods of shallower breathing, tidal volume was reduced by over 50% in NMNΔ6910KO mice.
source: During the periods of shallower breathing, tidal volume (the amount of air inhaled during a single breath) was reduced by over 50%, while the frequency of breathing was variable but not statistically different from control (Figure 1e).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1e showing quantified tidal volume.

claim: The frequency of breathing in NMNΔ6910KO mice was variable but not statistically different from control.
source: During the periods of shallower breathing, tidal volume (the amount of air inhaled during a single breath) was reduced by over 50%, while the frequency of breathing was variable but not statistically different from control (Figure 1e).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1e showing quantified breathing frequency.

claim: NMN∆ mice likely die due to deficiencies in feeding.
source: While NMN∆ mice likely die due to deficiencies in feeding (data not shown), NMNΔ6910KO mice appear cyanotic and gasp for breath (Figure 1b, Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: This is a statement based on unpublished observations (data not shown).

claim: Burst frequency was highly variable and irregular even in control mice at e18.5/P0, as the respiratory rhythm has not yet stabilized.
source: Burst frequency was highly variable and irregular even in control mice at e18.5/P0, as the respiratory rhythm has not yet stabilized (Hilaire and Duron, 1999), precluding meaningful analysis of respiratory burst frequency amongst different cadherin mutants.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hilaire and Duron, 1999.

claim: Latent non-respiratory propriospinal networks can activate phrenic MNs in a pattern that is distinct from respiratory bursts under disinhibitory conditions.
source: While not normally detectable, latent non-respiratory propriospinal networks can activate phrenic MNs in a pattern that is distinct from respiratory bursts under disinhibitory conditions (Cregg et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cregg et al., 2017.

claim: Spinal cord-initiated phrenic MN activity is of lower amplitude and longer duration than respiratory bursts, and persists after C1 transection eliminates descending inputs from brainstem respiratory centers.
source: This spinal cord-initiated phrenic MN activity is of lower amplitude and longer duration than respiratory bursts, and persists after C1 transection eliminates descending inputs from brainstem respiratory centers.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about spinal network activity.

claim: The rVRG is the major monosynaptic input to phrenic MNs.
source: To test whether cadherins are also required in presynaptic partners of PMC neurons to generate robust respiratory output, we performed in situ hybridization to define cadherin expression in the rVRG, the major monosynaptic input neurons to phrenic MNs (Wu et al., 2017), at e15.5, when rVRG to PMC connectivity is being established.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wu et al., 2017.

claim: The excitatory interneurons in both the preBötC and the rVRG arise from the Dbx1+, p0 progenitor domain.
